name: BPC-157
lead: BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound 157, also called bepecin or PL 14736) is a synthetic peptide of fifteen amino acids whose sequence is derived from a protein found in human gastric juice. It was first described by the pharmacologist Predrag Sikiric and colleagues at the University of Zagreb in the early 1990s, and nearly all of the published research on it comes from animal experiments, a large share of them from that group [1][12].

In fitness, injury-recovery and looksmaxxing circles it is promoted for healing tendons, ligaments, muscle and the gut, and is typically obtained as a research peptide or through compounding channels. Proponents describe it as a recovery aid that might support training and physique goals; the evidence cited for this is overwhelmingly rodent data, and reviews repeatedly note that efficacy in humans has not been confirmed [1][5][8].

No drug regulator has approved BPC-157 for human use. Published reviews describe human data as extremely limited, consisting of a few small pilot or retrospective studies and one phase 1 registration whose results were not submitted [1][8]. Its legal and regulatory position has been shifting; Wikipedia reports that on 30 October 2026 the US Health Secretary announced it, along with several other peptides, could be supplied by compounding pharmacies, while stating this does not make it an approved drug [1].

paras: BPC-157 is a linear peptide with the sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val. It is described as a fragment of a larger gastric protein and is unusually stable, remaining intact in human gastric juice for more than 24 hours in the account given by Wikipedia [1]. In rodent models it has been reported to be active after intramuscular, intravenous, oral, intraperitoneal and topical administration [1][4].
A urine test based on weak cation exchange solid-phase extraction has been described, and the peptide was reported to be stable in urine for four days [1].

BPC-157 is not marketed for cosmetic purposes in the way topical products are. In appearance and training communities it is discussed as a way to speed recovery from tendon, ligament, muscle and joint injuries, so that training can continue, and some users also report it for gut complaints and, anecdotally, for conditions such as tinnitus [19][20][21][22][23].
Orthopaedic reviews note that clinicians and athletes increasingly use it despite its lack of approval and its prohibition in professional sport [6].

There are no approved medical uses. Wikipedia notes it has been used in functional medicine without regulatory approval, and that some jurisdictions have restricted it as a prescription-only medicine even though it is not available through legitimate prescription [1].

Laboratory work attributes several actions to BPC-157. In cell and chick-membrane assays it increased vessel density and activated VEGFR2, supporting a pro-angiogenic role [10]. In cultured tendon fibroblasts it raised growth hormone receptor expression [11] and promoted outgrowth, survival and migration of tendon cells [9]. A 2025 narrative review summarises the proposed pathways as VEGFR2 signalling, nitric oxide synthesis through Akt-eNOS, and ERK1/2 signalling, with anti-inflammatory effects [8].

Sikiric's group has long described an interaction with the nitric oxide system, reporting that BPC 157 counteracted lesions produced by NOS inhibition in rats [4][12]. These mechanistic claims come from preclinical work and have not been confirmed in controlled human studies [5][8].

Wikipedia states BPC-157 is bioavailable in rodent models when given intramuscularly or intravenously [1]. A 2025 systematic review in an orthopaedic journal set out to cover metabolism and safety alongside mechanism, but human pharmacokinetic data are sparse [6].

Reviews of the animal literature describe consistent positive findings. A 2019 review of musculoskeletal studies reported prompt healing across tendon, ligament and muscle injury models, while stressing that most work used small rodent models, that only a handful of research groups had published in depth, and that efficacy in humans was not yet confirmed [5]. A 2018 review concluded that BPC 157 was consistently effective across a range of gastrointestinal injury models in animals when given alone [4]. A 2021 review covers rat skin wounds, burns and diabetic ulcers [7].

Individual studies include an alkali-burn wound model in rats where topical treatment accelerated wound closure [14], and early work from 1994 comparing it with H2 receptor antagonists in rat gastric and duodenal lesion models [13].

In humans, the evidence base is much smaller. A 2025 scoping review identified only three pilot studies in people, covering intra-articular knee pain, interstitial cystitis and intravenous administration [8]. Wikipedia describes a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain and a phase 1 trial in healthy volunteers whose results were not submitted [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports similar small studies including a 16-patient knee retrospective review and a 12-patient interstitial cystitis study [2]. Reviewers consistently describe the human evidence as too limited to establish efficacy [3][6][8].

Controlled human trials are scarce. Published reports are limited to small pilot or retrospective studies, as summarised in a 2025 scoping review [8] and in Wikipedia's account of a 12-patient knee pain study and an unreported phase 1 trial [1]. A systematic review of the orthopaedic sports-medicine literature identified 544 articles from 1993 to 2024 in total, the great majority being preclinical [6].

Several trials are registered. A phase 1 trial of BPC-157 for recovery after rotator cuff repair (NCT07803250, planned n=30) was listed as not yet recruiting, with a start date in 2027 [15]. A phase 2 trial of BPC-157 for acute hamstring muscle strain (NCT07437547, n=120) was listed as recruiting from February 2026 [16]. A phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetics registration in healthy volunteers (NCT02637284, n=42) has an unknown status [17]. A small completed trial of peptide gummies on markers of inflammation and post-exercise recovery (NCT07752381, n=40) has also been registered; results were not available in the sources reviewed [18]. Registrations are not results, and none of these has published efficacy findings that could be cited here.

A 2025 patent and literature review states that few side effects have been reported and describes a favourable safety profile in animals, while also noting that the lack of comprehensive human studies is why regulators have not approved it [3]. A 2021 review notes no reported toxicity in the animal work (an LD1 was not reached) [7].

Wikipedia notes a theoretical concern: because the compound promotes angiogenesis, it might promote cancer or enlarge undetected cancers [1]. A 2025 narrative review of musculoskeletal use similarly lists safety concerns alongside regenerative potential and notes that human data are extremely limited [8]. Health authorities discourage use because human safety data are insufficient [1].
Products sold as research peptides are unregulated; questions about purity, identity and contamination apply, as raised in general reviews of gray-market injectable peptides.

The peptide emerged from Croatian research on the protective role of gastric juice. A 1993 overview in the Journal of Physiology (Paris) described a gastric-juice peptide called BPC and the 'stomach-stress-organoprotection' hypothesis [12]. In 1994 the 15-amino-acid fragment BPC 157 was reported to protect against stress-, cysteamine- and ethanol-induced gastric and duodenal lesions in rats [13].

Through the 1990s and 2000s the group published studies on the nitric oxide system, NSAID toxicity, colitis and wound healing in rats [4][7]. Interest in tendon healing followed, with work from other groups, including a 2011 study of tendon fibroblast outgrowth and migration [9] and a 2014 study on growth hormone receptor expression [11]. Later reviews noted that over two decades only a handful of groups had performed in-depth studies [5].

BPC-157 is not approved by any drug regulatory agency. Wikipedia states it is controlled as a prescription medicine in jurisdictions such as New Zealand and Australia despite not actually being available by prescription [1].

In sport, Wikipedia reports it has been banned by WADA since 2022 under the S0 category of non-exempt substances [1]. A 2025 review puts it differently, stating that it was temporarily banned in 2022 and is not currently listed [3]; sources therefore differ and the status may change.

Wikipedia reports that on 30 October 2026 the US Health Secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., announced that BPC-157, TB-500, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c and semax would be permitted to be supplied by compounding pharmacies despite lack of FDA approval [1]. Grokipedia, which is AI-generated and may contain errors, describes the policy as enforcement discretion for State-licensed pharmacies and licensed physicians under section 503A, with conditions such as a certificate of analysis, single-ingredient products, adverse-event reporting and a patient-specific prescription, and states it does not make BPC-157 an approved drug. Grokipedia also reports earlier steps, including a Category 2 bulk-substance classification in 2023 and an advisory committee vote in 2026 [2].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: On the T Nation forum, BPC-157 appears frequently in training logs and injury threads. Users describe injecting it near an injured joint or muscle, and pair it with TB-500 [19][20][21]. Posters say it helped with tennis elbow, muscle tears or post-surgical recovery [20][21][22]. Others describe it more cautiously: one poster calls it a lubricant that helps promote healing and notes it is nothing like growth hormone [24], and another says its strength is not inflammation [19].

Vendors typically label the product for research purposes only, and forum users refer to purchasing it on that basis [21]. Grokipedia reports a surge in popularity during 2025 and 2026 driven by social media and public figures, which is an unverified claim from an AI-generated source [2].

Ongoing registrations in rotator cuff repair and hamstring strain suggest the first controlled human trials in sports-injury settings [15][16]. Reviewers call for well-designed clinical trials and independent replication outside the original research group before conclusions about efficacy in humans can be drawn [5][6][8].

timeline.event: Sikiric and colleagues publish an overview of a gastric-juice peptide called BPC in the Journal of Physiology (Paris). [12]
The 15-amino-acid fragment BPC 157 is reported to protect against experimental gastric and duodenal lesions in rats. [13]
A study reports that BPC 157 promotes tendon fibroblast outgrowth, survival and migration in culture. [9]
BPC 157 is reported to raise growth hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts. [11]
A study links BPC 157 to VEGFR2 activation and angiogenesis. [10]
WADA prohibition is reported by Wikipedia; a 2025 review describes it as temporary. [1][3]
Systematic and scoping reviews find very limited human data. [6][8]
Wikipedia reports a US announcement permitting compounding pharmacy supply of BPC-157 and other peptides (30 October). [1]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar fitness forums, BPC-157 is one of the most commonly mentioned recovery peptides, usually discussed alongside TB-500 for injuries and surgery recovery. [19][20]

claims.claim: BPC-157 heals tendon and muscle injuries much faster than normal.
claims.believers: Users report that it 'does wonders' for injuries and say it helped tennis elbow, quad and hamstring problems and post-surgical recovery [20][21][22]. One post frames it as a signal that makes the body repair itself rather than adding a hormone [20].
claims.experts: Animal studies report faster healing in tendon, ligament and muscle injury models, but reviewers say most work was in small rodent models from a few groups and that efficacy in humans is not confirmed [5][8].

claims.claim: BPC-157 and TB-500 work synergistically as a 'recovery stack'.
claims.believers: Forum posts describe injecting both near an injury and say the combination is better than either alone [19][21].
claims.experts: No published controlled human trial of the combination was identified in the reviews consulted, and human data on BPC-157 alone are described as extremely limited [8].

claims.claim: It is safe because there are almost no reported side effects.
claims.believers: Posters describe it as low-risk and note that it is not a steroid [21].
claims.experts: Reviews describe few reported side effects and a favourable animal safety profile, but state that human safety data are minimal and that its pro-angiogenic activity raises a theoretical cancer concern [1][3][8].

claims.claim: BPC-157 helps with other problems such as tinnitus or gut conditions.
claims.believers: A forum poster says they heard good things about BPC-157 for tinnitus [23]; gut-healing claims are also common in the community.
claims.experts: Gastrointestinal healing is the origin of the research, with positive results in rat colitis and ulcer models [4]; no controlled human trials support tinnitus or gut claims [8].

claims.claim: Doctors do not prescribe it because it 'makes you better' and is not profitable.
claims.believers: A forum poster asks why doctors do not prescribe it if it could halve surgical recovery time [20].
claims.experts: Regulators and reviews attribute the lack of approval to the absence of sufficient clinical studies confirming benefit in humans [3].
